research_text:
# Research brief: `java.security.MessageDigest` and the finding "expecting one of SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512 but found SHA1"

## Source limits

- **I could not retrieve the rule file itself.** I have no page-fetch tool, and the sandbox has no network access. The raw `MessageDigest.crysl` URL you gave was never opened.
- **No verbatim clause from the master file.** I have no text from the current master revision, so I cannot quote the matching clause from it. Question 4 is only partly answerable.
- **What I could read instead:**
  - web-search excerpts of the CrySL papers;
  - the CROSSINGTUD GitHub landing pages, which show the folder layout but not the rule contents;
  - Oracle's Javadoc and security guides, which came back as excerpts rather than full pages.
- **Discrepancies in your input:**
  - The finding text lists six accepted names (`SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, `SHA-512`, `SHA256`, `SHA384`, `SHA512`). The rule as you summarized it, and as printed in the 2018 CrySL paper, lists only three hyphenated names.
  - The finding says `SHA1`, while your summary says `SHA-1`.
  - The paper's protocol (`Gets, (d2 | (Updates+, Digests)), …`) differs from the protocol in your input.
  - Together these suggest the rule revision the scanner bundled differs from both the paper and your summary. This is unresolved.

## Q1. What `MessageDigest` governs, and what the finding refers to

- The JCA Reference Guide describes `MessageDigest` as an engine class that provides cryptographically secure message digests such as SHA-256 or SHA-512. <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html>
- The class is obtained through its `getInstance` methods. <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html>
  - `getInstance(String algorithm)` returns an object implementing the named digest.
  - `getInstance(String algorithm, Provider provider)` does the same for a specific provider.
  - The Javadoc says the name should be a standard Java Security name, such as "SHA-256".
- The API's event vocabulary is:
  - `update(byte)`, `update(byte[])`, `update(byte[],int,int)` and `update(ByteBuffer)`;
  - `digest()`, `digest(byte[])` and `digest(byte[],int,int)`;
  - `reset()` and the static `isEqual`.
  - <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html>
- A finding of this form refers to the String algorithm-name argument of `getInstance`. The detector message describes that value as `SHA1`.
- `SHA1` is not the standard name. The standard name list gives "SHA-1" (160-bit digest). <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html>
- The sources I read do not say whether `SHA1` resolves as an alias in the JDK providers. The JDK Providers page excerpt I saw shows OIDs but no alias list. <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/security/oracleproviders.htm>

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and recommended remediation

- **Standard usage.** The JCA guide's examples request `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`, and optionally name a provider, then compute the digest. <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html>
- **Lifecycle** (<https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html> and the Java 5 Javadoc at <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/1.5.0/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html>):
  - A digest object starts initialized.
  - `digest(byte[])` performs a final update and then completes the computation.
  - After any `digest` call the object resets to its initialized state.
- **Comparison.** The Java 5 Javadoc says `isEqual` does a simple byte compare. <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/1.5.0/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html> The excerpts I read do not say whether current versions are constant-time. I did not verify this.
- **No official remediation text.** In the excerpts I read, the Javadoc and JCA guide do not call SHA-1 unsafe and do not recommend a replacement for it.
  - SHA-1 is still a listed standard name in Java 8 and in current Java, defined by FIPS 180-4. <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html>
  - I found no official `MessageDigest` text that says "replace SHA-1 with X". Any such guidance would come from the rule or from NIST, not from the Java API documentation.
- **NIST guidance** (<https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions/nist-policy-on-hash-functions>):
  - Federal agencies should stop using SHA-1 for digital signatures, time stamps, and other uses that need collision resistance.
  - They may still use it to verify old signatures and for HMAC, key derivation functions (KDFs) and random-number generation.
  - NIST names SHA-2 or SHA-3 as the alternative.
  - FIPS 140 modules with SHA-1 approval move to the historical list after 12/31/2030.
  - This is NIST policy for US federal agencies, not a Java API statement.
- **Fit with your policy rules.** NIST's use-dependent treatment matches your first rule: classify the digest's purpose before judging impact. The Java documentation gives no classification.

## Q3. Compatibility when the algorithm is changed

- **Persisted and wire formats.**
  - I found no official Java statement about persisted or wire formats for `MessageDigest` output.
  - What the documentation does say is that SHA-1 produces a 160-bit digest, SHA-256 a 256-bit digest, SHA-384 a 384-bit digest and SHA-512 a 512-bit digest. The output length is fixed per algorithm. <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html>
  - Any stored or transmitted digest from a different algorithm therefore cannot match. The documentation does not discuss the consequences. That is a deployment question these sources do not answer.
- **Platform version support.**
  - Java 7 lists SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 as names. <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html>
  - The Java 8 implementation-requirements table lists MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 as required for every Java SE implementation. SHA-384 and SHA-512 are defined names but do not appear in that required list. <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html>
  - The requirements table in the current Java 25 excerpt was truncated ("SHA-1 SHA-256 SHA-384…"), so I cannot state its full contents.
  - The Standard Names document says these requirements do not apply to third-party providers.
  - The JDK 8 table does not require SHA-384 or SHA-512, but I did not find a statement that the JDK's own providers lack them.
- **JDK handling of SHA-1** (these settings do not govern `MessageDigest.getInstance`):
  - JEP 288 concerns SHA-1 certificates and signed JARs, via `jdk.certpath.disabledAlgorithms` and `jdk.jar.disabledAlgorithms`. <https://openjdk.org/jeps/288>
  - The JDK 11.0.9 release notes say the `jdk.security.legacyAlgorithms` property drives warnings in keytool and jarsigner, and that SHA-1 is among the algorithms warned about. <https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-0-9-relnotes.html>
  - I found no documented JDK property that blocks `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")`.
- **Migration path.** I found no official migration guide for a `MessageDigest` algorithm change.
- **Fit with your policy rules.** The policy's rule about unchanged external contracts needs evidence from the consumer of the digest, which these sources do not provide.

## Q4. What the rule matches

Only part of this can be answered from sources I read.

**What the 2018 paper shows.**
- Fig. 10 shows the algorithm constraint as `algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};`. That is a closed allow-list, with only those three hyphenated names.
- The paper's own example uses MD5 as the violating value, to show that the rule forbids MD5.
- Sources:
  - <https://www.bodden.de/pubs/tse19CrySL.pdf>
  - <https://bodden.de/pubs/ksa+18crysl.pdf>
  - <https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol109-ecoop2018/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10.pdf>
- This is the 2018 paper's figure, not the master file you cited. It is not a verbatim clause from your rule revision.

**CrySL language semantics from the same paper.**
- A rule starts with a `SPEC` line naming the class it governs.
- The `EVENTS` section lists the method signatures that may contribute to correct use.
- Each signature includes the method name and its argument types.
- On those semantics, a signature-based event is tied to the method name plus its argument types. It also appears tied to the `SPEC` type, so a same-named method on a different class would not be in scope.

**What I cannot state from sources:**
- The exact method names and receiver types in the master file.
- Whether the master file's `getInstance` events constrain the parameter list. By the language definition they would include argument types, but I did not see the file.
- How the analyzer (CogniCrypt/CryptoAnalysis) resolves receiver types. This is outside what I read.
- The answer to your explicit question, whether the rule can match a method that merely shares a name with the governed API. By language semantics the answer appears to be no, but I cannot confirm it from the rule file.
- The condition evaluated on a matched call. The paper's Fig. 10 shows a membership test on `algorithm`. The six-name list in your finding implies the master file differs.

## Unresolved

1. The verbatim `EVENTS` and `CONSTRAINTS` clauses of the master `MessageDigest.crysl`, and the revision the scanner bundled.
2. Whether `SHA1` and `SHA-1` are treated identically by the detector, and by the JDK's providers.
3. Whether any official Java document gives remediation text for SHA-1 in `MessageDigest`. I found none.
4. Any official statement on persisted or wire-format migration for digests. I found none.
